activity.title: A year ago, I probably would’ve laughed if you told me I’d be spending my summer trying to build a new approach to computing. But here we are. Excited to share that I’ve joined Entrepreneur First’s San Francisco fellowship program to continue building Sumeru Quantum! At Sumeru, we’re exploring a new approach to computing using superconducting digital logic, with the goal of building significantly more energy-efficient compute infrastructure for AI and HPC. We’ve been moving quickly from architecture to hardware, developing circuit-level simulations, designing our first superconducting test structures, and working toward fabrication and experimental validation. Along the way, I’ve had the opportunity to work with and learn from researchers and engineers across superconducting electronics, fabrication, and high-performance computing. Excited for what’s ahead 📈

You can't wait for opportunities to come your way, you have to push for them. I'm wrapping up my internship at IBM next week, and the biggest thing that's earned me recognition isn't what was assigned to me, it's what I pushed and advocated for. Earlier this summer, there was a US-wide IBM Sales intern hackathon. My team and I grinded out our project, troubleshot, and iterated as much as we could. And we lost. 😅 But that's not where the story ends. We knew we had something special, something people would really find useful, so we pushed to keep working on it. 💡 After a few weeks of more work and guidance from our mentor, we were ready for launch. Last week, Shreyas Sambara , Aarav Singh , and I presented our project to Solutions Engineers across the entire US. We targeted a real need and presented a solution. 🎯 We left thinking that was that. We'd maybe grow our tool through grassroots efforts: asking for feedback, pushing for usage, and just being proactive. What really happened was our project got noticed by senior managers, and they were impressed. As of now, we're integrating our project into an internal tool hosted in the Office of the CIO. 📈 So what's the takeaway, to prove I'm not just bragging? Real effort goes a long way. When you're faced with a challenge, don't just do a half-good job to get it done. Really see how you can change and improve things for the better. It could end up getting you noticed. __________________________________________ From a future tech leader (we're manifesting 🤩) Follow Maxim (Max) Yurkovsky for my journey navigating entry level tech

Sidekick (YC S26) is an AI agent that handles frontline operations over text – no app, no login, no training. In a manufacturing plant, critical knowledge is scattered everywhere – binders on a shelf, a supervisor's head, systems no one on the line can log into. None of it is reachable from the floor, so when a machine goes down or a spec is unclear, the line stops while someone goes looking. Sidekick pulls all of it into one centralized knowledge base that every worker can reach by text. Workers text questions and get answers grounded in their company's own SOPs. They text problems and work orders get created. When Sidekick can't answer, the question escalates to a manager and the answer is saved – so the knowledge base grows with every question, and the tribal knowledge that usually walks out the door when a veteran retires stays with the company. Founder Justin So worked in his father's manufacturing business and witnessed the problem firsthand. Sidekick is now live on manufacturing floors in 4 countries and serving hundreds of workers. Congrats on the launch, Justin! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gyPv9AwV

Two weeks ago, I finally got the courage to record myself and post it on Instagram. For the past few months, I’ve been quietly working on Trajecta , an AI college consulting tool that helps students from 9-12th grade plan ahead for their college applications. I would put in hours every day adding new features, revising old UI, and testing output accuracy. But then something dawned on me. What do any of these iterations and continuous building even mean if nobody actually uses it? I’ve been avoiding the biggest and most uncomfortable part of creating a saas tool these days: marketing. And so a month ago, I decided to finally make some faceless content on TikTok. Most of the videos were funny videos related to colleges that only mentioned Trajecta at the very end of the video. These videos all performed very well, and after just four videos, I garnered over 500k+ views, and one of them even got reposted and went viral on X. Yet despite the traction, only around 20 people actually signed up to our website, and I became demotivated again and stopped posting. Two weeks ago, that changed. I finally decided to post videos with my face talking to the camera. I hate listening to my voice and videos of myself, but if I never got over the hump of posting and learning how to make content, my product would not get any trust, and I would just continue adding more features that no one would ever use. And it’s working. After just two weeks, I garnered over 300k views and 300+ followers, while my website finally got real paying users. I’m not posting every day yet. I’m not doing any fancy editing tricks. But I already broke through the toughest challenge I've faced these past few months. If you want to take a look at my new videos, go check out @yimingbuilds on Instagram. Still figuring things out, but more will be coming soon!

I'm taking a break from content creation. Let me explain. 1. Lately when I create, I've been feeling a lack of fulfillment. Writing and filming posts became more of a task than something I was passionate about, and for that reason I don't think it was something worth keeping in my routine even though my social media pages were growing. 2. I love engineering. I love it so much right now that I would rather spend those extra few hours of my day learning more about engineering than working on a video or post. 3. Content made me feel like I was making progress when I wasn't. The dopamine / validation that I get when I post about accomplishments, goals, and projects made me feel like I was achieving more than I actually was. This hindered my execution speed and urgency. I still intend to post. The difference is that I will only post when I have inspiration behind it, not because I wanted to meet a weekly quota. I think too much of content can become a performance and chasing numbers. So, I am trying to slow down on the personal branding to build myself up and stay authentic.

In 2004, Sal Khan 's 12-year-old cousin Nadia was placed into her school's slower math track. She told him, “I'm just not a math person.” Khan, a hedge fund analyst with 3 degrees from Massachusetts Institute of Technology , knew that one placement in middle school follows you for life. He made her a deal: if she'd give him half an hour a day after school, he'd tutor her over the phone and Yahoo Doodle. In the first two weeks, Nadia answered every math question with a question mark in her voice. "What's two to the third power?" She'd say, "Eight?" So Khan spent those sessions teaching her to say "eight" with confidence and conviction. Then he started teaching her math concepts ahead of her class, like negative exponents. When she understood them, he told her, "By the way, you're a 7th grader doing 10th grade math right now." She replied, "Really?" Khan called Nadia's school about retaking the placement exam. She moved from the remedial track to the advanced track. Word spread through the family. Soon Khan was tutoring 15 cousins across three time zones. A friend suggested he record the lessons for YouTube . Khan laughed: "YouTube is for cats playing piano, not for serious mathematics." He uploaded anyway. His entire studio was a walk-in closet, a $20 screen recorder, and Microsoft Paint. Viewers never saw his face, just heard a voice and watched equations fill the screen. Then Khan received a letter from a parent. Their 12-year-old son had autism, and every tutoring program they'd tried had failed him. Khan's recordings were the first resource that worked. Today, Khan Academy has nearly 190 million registered users. Nadia was taking university-level calculus by ninth grade. In a world where systems label us too early, conviction and support in another person's potential is the most underrated force. Be the person who offers it generously.

We’ve decided to open-source a multi-agent harness we use internally at YC. We call it “QM” and it’s meant to be easy to customize, like Hermes or OpenClaw, but useful for a whole company. We use it across accounting, legal, events, and engineering (including building QM itself!). The whole project is under an MIT license. It is cloud-first and has Slack and web UI natively. Some features: • Triggers (crons, webhooks), memory, shared files • Connectors for a company brain • Agent browser support • Shareable web app artifacts • Multi-player projects Like many things we do at YC, it’s an experiment. It’s early and has bugs. But it’s been surprisingly useful for us so far, and we’re excited to share it and get feedback from the community. If you want to host it yourself, try telling your coding agent of choice to “deploy https://github[.]com/yc-software/qm” (remove the brackets!)
